chapter_title: A Catechumen asked the Apostle: When I would give
spiritual_reading:
# Spiritual Translation — The Parable of the Enemy and the Physician

---

**¶4:**

For this matter is likened unto two spiritual agencies: if falsity from evil — an adversary and opponent to the life of the mind — should first assault a person and inflict corruption and injury upon his external life, and afterwards should assault him again and [GAP-1: compound the damage upon him], striking over the same corruptions with further falsities, and [GAP-2: reopening the] injuries that had already implanted evils in him, and [GAP-3: so] assaults him these two times — [GAP-4: then the injured one] brings accusation against the falsity from evil that has assaulted him. And divine truth in its judicial capacity examines that adversary directly concerning the [GAP-5: nature and severity] of the corruptions that it has left as permanent effects upon his external life. And they [GAP-6: judge the charge against] it as though it had destroyed his inmost understanding. And it is brought before judgment and sentence, and is condemned before the Lord who governs divine order in the natural degree. Divine justice exacts consequence for each corruption in the very faculty where it was inflicted, and adds to it the injury that the adversary had imposed upon this one who had committed no evil against it. The law of spiritual consequence upon the adversary shall not be omitted, as it is judged [GAP-7: and condemned] according to the degree of its opposition to good.

---

**¶5:**

After the completion of this judgment, the falsity from evil is condemned according to the full measure of spiritual consequence [GAP-8: for its] transgression against him. Afterwards, the one who was assaulted remains in spiritual illness [GAP-9: even after the condemnation of] the adversary that struck him, and an evil manifests openly upon him [GAP-10: from within his damaged state], and he becomes one afflicted by reason of his spiritual disease, and he [GAP-11: seeks remedy for it.] He turns to divine truth in its healing capacity and reveals to it his spiritual wound. However, that healing truth bears no [GAP-12: enmity toward him] nor [GAP-13: malice of any kind], and it takes discriminating truth to him and opens this evil. Nevertheless, when it opens it, the vital truths of his life pour forth from the wound. That person shall suffer the pain of reformation, but he accepts both the cutting and the outpouring. This healing truth has not retaliated nor was any harm imputed to it; because it did this to him for the restoration of his spiritual wholeness. All that it did to him was done from the good and for the good; and not at all from evil purpose.

---

**¶6:**

After the completion of the process, it opens this evil fully and draws forth the falsified life from it and restores health to the whole faculty. It shall even bring forth [GAP-14: gratitude and acknowledgment from the one healed, who offers] tokens of thankfulness and praise. That spiritual disease and its healing become a glory belonging to divine truth in its restorative office, and it is given honor and worship.

---

**¶8:**

Also, [GAP-15: consider how this corresponds to] the other agency — [GAP-16: the adversary who] assaulted the companion of the [GAP-17: one made spiritually] ill by means of his [GAP-18: malice —] who struck in [GAP-19: opposition to good,] being cruel according to [GAP-20: enmity against the] living affection of the soul [GAP-21: and inflicting evil] upon it, [GAP-22: so that] that [GAP-23: one suffers under the] accusation of [GAP-24: divine justice for the evil done.]

---

*Note on ¶8:* This passage is heavily lacunose. The spiritual sense requires a return to the contrast between the adversary (falsity from evil acting from enmity) and the healer (divine truth acting from love). The fragments — "cruel," "living soul," "accusation" — anchor the reading: falsity from evil acts with cruelty against the living affection itself, and for this it stands under the full accusation of divine order. The gaps resist certainty in their exact wording, but the spiritual trajectory is clear.

reconstructions.reconstructed_text: For this matter is like to two people, if a personal enemy and an opponent of theirs will hit one first and make a sore and a wound on his body. Afterwards he smites him again and [wounds him] and he hits over his blows and [opens the] blows that have made sores on him and [after he] strikes him these two times [that one] accuses his enemy who has struck him. And this judge questions him to his face about the [matter] of the sores that he has left as marks on his body. And they [lay the charge] on him as if he had split his head. And he is led to judgement and sentence, and is punished before the judge of the world. He makes retribution for a sore in the sore place, and adds to him the wound that he had left on this person who had not yet sinned against him. He shall not omit the retaliation of the opponent, as he is judged [and condemned] according to enmity.

After the end, this enemy is condemned for the retaliation [of his] sin against him. Afterwards, the other one is sick [he being] the one whom this enemy has struck, and a wound comes out on him [from within] and he becomes a sick person by cause of his illness, and he [seeks healing] He calls the doctor and shows him his wound. However, that doctor has no [enmity with him] nor [malice] and he takes the knife to him and cuts this wound. Nevertheless, when he cuts it the blood shall pour out of his wound. That person shall be pained, but he accepts those and these things. This doctor has not retaliated nor was harm imposed on him; because he did this thing to him for healing his wound. All that he did to him was done for the good; and not directly for evil.

After the completion, he cuts this wound and lets blood from it and heals it. He shall even make [him] gifts and compliments. That illness and the healing become a pride for this doctor, and he is given honour.

Also, [this] is the other person [who] struck the comrade of the [one made] sick with his [enmity] he struck in [evil] he being cruel according to [his enmity against the] living soul [and inflicting evil] upon it [...] that [he bears the] accusation of [the judge]

fills.explanation: The enemy compounds the original injury by striking and wounding again, paralleling the earlier "make a sore and a wound on his body."
The spiritual sense of "reopening the injuries" requires an active verb; "opens the blows that have made sores" describes aggravating existing wounds.
The spiritual reading indicates a consequential "so" — the temporal connector "after he" transitions from the assault to the accusation that follows.
The spiritual reading specifies "then the injured one" as the subject who brings accusation; "that one" identifies the victim in the Kephalaia's impersonal register.
The judge inquires about the "matter" (nature and extent) of the sores — standard judicial language in the Kephalaia for examining the full character of an injury.
The spiritual reading says "judge the charge against" him; in the text's legal-parable register, "lay the charge on him" introduces the formal accusation before sentencing.
The standard judicial pair "judged and condemned" completes the sentencing formula; the spiritual reading confirms "and condemned" according to the degree of enmity.
The enemy is condemned for the retaliation proportional to "his sin" — the connective "of his" links the retaliation to the enemy's specific transgression.
An appositive construction identifying "the other one" as the same person whom the enemy struck; even after judgment on the enemy, the victim remains sick.
The spiritual reading specifies the wound manifests "from within his damaged state"; in the text's register, the wound emerges "from within" the body, indicating latent corruption surfacing.

The spiritual reading says the afflicted one "seeks remedy for it," and the next sentence has him calling the doctor — "seeks healing" bridges the recognition of illness to the act of summoning the physician.
The spiritual reading specifies the doctor bears no "enmity toward him"; the physician acts without the hostile relation that characterized the enemy in ¶4.
The spiritual reading says "malice of any kind" as the second member of the pair with enmity; "no enmity nor malice" is a standard doublet expressing complete absence of hostile intent.
The healed person makes the doctor gifts — "him" is the indirect object referring to the physician who receives gratitude and acknowledgment for the healing.
The editor's "this" correctly serves as the demonstrative introducing the identification of the parable's figure: "Also, this is the other person."
The editor's "who" correctly functions as the relative pronoun: "the other person who struck the comrade," identifying the adversary's action.
The spiritual reading says "one made spiritually ill"; in the text's natural register, "the comrade of the one made sick" identifies the victim through the enemy's action.
The spiritual reading specifies "malice" as the instrument; in the Kephalaia's register, "enmity" is the natural-plane term for hostile intent that characterizes the enemy throughout the chapter.
The spiritual reading says "opposition to good"; in the text's register, "he struck in evil" denotes the mode of assault — acting from evil purpose, contrasted with the physician who acts for good.

The spiritual reading specifies "enmity against the living affection"; "being cruel according to his enmity against the living soul" connects cruelty to its root cause — hostile opposition to living good.
The spiritual reading says "and inflicting evil upon it"; this describes the active imposition of harm upon the living soul, continuing the description of the enemy's assault.
The spiritual reading says "one suffers under the accusation"; "that he bears the accusation" expresses the enemy standing under judgment for the evil done.
The spiritual reading says "divine justice for the evil done"; "accusation of the judge" echoes the "judge of the world" from ¶4, denoting divine order's formal charge against the enemy.
